explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on list- or bullet-style “catalog” language—brief, itemized descriptions of services, products or specifications (often with URLs, metadata like ISBNs or dates, and marketing/promo phrasing).

This feature flags document‐structure metadata markers—words and phrases that signal section headings or post metadata (e.g. “ABSTRACT:” in a paper or “This entry was posted…,” dates, “filed under,” “RSS,” etc. in a blog footer).
This feature is essentially a “terminal‐period” detector—it lights up on tokens that are a dot (or include a trailing dot), marking the end of an abbreviation, title initial, heading or sentence.
This neuron fires whenever the model sees the leading fragment of a capitalized name or entity (i.e. the subword prefix of a surname, organization, etc.).

This feature fires on the hallmarks of a cooking‐recipe step—things like the numbered/“bullet” formatting (e.g. “2.” or sentence-ending “.”), imperative cooking verbs (“stir,” “refrigerate,” “preheat”), and ingredient nouns or descriptors (“coconut,” “cocoa,” “white flour,” etc.)—essentially marking “this is a recipe instruction” at the token level.

This neuron responds to tokens that anchor a statement in time or personal experience—numbers and adverbs/phrases like “15,” “once,” “back,” “ever,” “used to,” etc., that set up a duration, past event or experiential frame.

This neuron is a cue for “noun‐phrase onset.”  It spikes on the definite article “the” (and occasionally an initial adjective like “late”) whenever a new NP (especially after a preposition or numeral) begins.

This neuron fires on typographic/emphatic cues—things like Markdown bold markers (`**…**`), runs of punctuation (e.g. “!!!!”), full-width or non-Latin characters used for emphasis, etc. In short, it detects formatting and emphasis markers rather than ordinary words.

This neuron is a discourse-structure detector: it lights up on the little “signpost” words and phrases—quantifiers, enumerators and cue-verbs—that introduce, compare or highlight key points (e.g. “more than,” “one thing,” “one of,” “among other things,” “provides,” “implore,” “how much,” etc.).
This neuron lights up on specialized technical/scientific entity tokens—acronyms, chemical formulas, gene- or protein-names, model/designation labels and similar domain-specific nomenclature.
